items.title: Gemini  4 Carbon is Truly Shocking: Benchmarks below.
items.summary:
Gemini  4 Carbon is Truly Shocking: Benchmarks below.

BROKEN DOWN INTO ITS INGREDIENTS

Google made Gemini 4 Carbon generally available on November 10, 2026, thirteen days after announcing it on October 28 and four weeks after Gemini 4 Argon shipped. The API model ID is gemini-4-carbon, the introductory price is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, and from December 1 the list price doubles to $4 and $20. Thinking tokens are billed as output.

This is a teardown of what Carbon is made of, built from what Google published (blog posts, the DeepMind model card, AI Studio docs) and what independent evaluators measured. Vendor claims are flagged, and undisclosed items are marked as such.

⚗️ The name: why Argon, then Carbon

Google has not publicly explained the element naming, so anything here is interpretation, not fact. The chemistry is still a useful mental model. Argon (Ar, atomic number 18) is a noble gas. It has a full outer electron shell and barely reacts with anything. Carbon (C, atomic number 6) has four valence electrons and forms four bonds, which is why it builds long chains, rings and the entire backbone of organic chemistry.

Mapped onto the two models, the analogy roughly holds. Google describes Argon as the efficient default for most coding and knowledge work. Carbon is the one built to chain long sequences of steps together, spend more tokens per turn and keep going for hours. Inside the Gemini app the picker labels make the split explicit: 4 Argon is tagged "Code & analysis" and 4 Carbon is tagged "Most complex work."

🧬 Ingredient 1: the base model

The DeepMind model card for Carbon is short on internals. Under Model dependencies it says one thing: Gemini 4 Carbon is based on Gemini 4 Argon. For architecture, training data, data processing, hardware and software, every section points back to the Argon model card.

The Argon card is more specific. It describes Argon as a large scale sparse mixture-of-experts transformer with native multimodal support for text, vision and audio inputs. It states Argon is a new model, not a fine-tune of an earlier Gemini. It was trained on Google TPUs using JAX and ML Pathways. Post-training used instruction tuning data, reinforcement learning data and human preference data, including RL on multi-step reasoning, problem solving and theorem proving data.

So the disclosed recipe is Argon's sparse MoE base plus additional post-training for deeper reasoning, longer verification loops and multi-step agent work.

What is not disclosed: total parameter count, active parameters per token, number of experts, the compute used for Carbon's extra post-training, and whether the serving stack differs from Argon. Independent trackers list all of these as undisclosed. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026 for both models. That is three months older than Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, which Anthropic lists at June 2026.

📐 Ingredient 2: context, output and modalities

From the AI Studio model page and the "What's new in Gemini 4 Carbon" guide:

Spec | Gemini 4 Carbon
Model ID | gemini-4-carbon
Inputs | Text, image, video, audio, PDF
Output | Text only
Context window | 1,048,576 tokens, unified input + thinking + output
Max output, synchronous | 65,536 tokens
Max output, long decode | Up to 1,048,576 minus input
Thinking levels | low, medium (default), high
Knowledge cutoff | March 2026

The unified window is the detail that changes how you budget. Input, thinking and output all draw from the same 1,048,576-token pool. If you send 600K tokens of repository context, the model has at most about 448K left for reasoning and answer combined.

Long decode is new for Gemini 4. A synchronous call stops at 65,536 tokens. Past that, set background=True and raise max_output_tokens. The server generates in 64K-token hops, each returned as a separate model_output step that your client joins.

Carbon does not generate images or audio and does not support the Live API.

🧠 Ingredient 3: thinking levels

The thinking level is the main quality, latency and cost control, and Carbon's defaults differ from earlier Gemini models in ways that break existing code.

Level | Token use | Google's guidance
low | Fewest, lowest latency | Simple and cost-sensitive work; quality can drop on hard tasks
medium | Balanced (default) | Most tasks, including complex code and agents
high | Most, slowest first token | Hard math, science, the hardest code and agent tasks

Three rules from the migration checklist. max_output_tokens caps thinking plus answer together, so a low cap can produce a truncated answer; Google recommends at least 32,768. temperature, top_p and top_k are ignored. Hard prompts can run for minutes, so use background execution or client timeouts of at least 15 minutes.

Artificial Analysis measured what the levels cost in practice. On its Intelligence Index, Carbon at low scored 54 and at medium scored 58, with output token use per task rising from 86.2K to 103K and reasoning tokens from 32.4K to 56.2K. Time to first token went from 12.15 seconds at low to 23.19 seconds at medium. Output speed was 64 to 73 tokens per second in that test. Other trackers report figures between about 85 and 95 tokens per second, so raw speed depends on load and endpoint. Whichever number you use, this is not a model for snappy chat.

🛠️ Ingredient 4: tools and consumption options

Carbon supports the full Gemini agent toolset: function calling, code execution, computer use, Google Search grounding, Google Maps grounding, URL context, file search, structured outputs and agentic video understanding. It runs on the Batch API, Flex inference and Priority inference.

Caching works differently from Gemini 3. Explicit caching (cachedContents, caches.create) is not supported. If your code creates or references cached_content, you have to remove it. Implicit caching is on by default for prompts of at least 4,096 tokens and gives a 95% discount on cache hits, which is $0.10 per million cached input tokens during the intro period and $0.20 after.

One caveat for the cost math: during Argon's launch, a heavy user publicly reported implicit cache hit rates of only 70 to 80%, against 99% or more elsewhere. That is anecdotal and unverified for Carbon, but if it carries over, effective input cost sits well above the cached rate.

Carbon also runs in Gemini Managed Agents via the Antigravity agent (antigravity-preview-09-2026). Google is previewing /swarm in Antigravity, which turns one prompt into a team of agents in parallel isolated workspaces: Carbon plans, coordinates and audits, lighter models do bulk work, and adversarial verifiers test each change.

🛡️ Ingredient 5: safety and cyber safeguards

Carbon's main selling point is cybersecurity, and that is also why access was staged. Google gave it first to a subset of cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program on October 28, said it was participating in the US government's voluntary pre-release testing process, and opened it to everyone else on November 10.

The most important footnote in the launch materials: Google says its cyber benchmark scores were "evaluated without guardrails," and the model card says the cyber results "reflect performance when accessed through the Fairwind Program." The specialized dual-use cyber capabilities are reserved for verified defenders. The public gemini-4-carbon endpoint runs with misuse safeguards on. So the 88.2% SEC-bench Pro score describes the Fairwind configuration, not necessarily what a normal API key gets on offensive-adjacent prompts.

Google's published safety numbers for Carbon:

Metric | Argon | Carbon
Per-attempt breach rate, adaptive red-team agent | 3.1% | 0.8%
Attack trajectories blocked (ExploitBench / CyScenarioBench envs) | not stated | 99%
Gray Swan automated cyberattack query success | 9.86% | 2.17%
Gray Swan indirect prompt injection attack success | 0.7% | 0.0%
Internal 375-task agentic honesty benchmark, tasks passed | 70% | 92%
Terminal-Bench 4.0 successful cheating | not stated | 0.0% (0.4% attempts)

Trajectory Labs found no new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests. Google also claims high-severity misalignment alerts in internal coding fell almost 80%, overreach fell 26% and under-service 29%.

Two honest qualifiers. Google itself writes that prompt injection robustness "remains an area for continued improvement" and that its red teaming found sophisticated attacks still succeed in some distributions, so a 0% score on one benchmark does not mean immune. Also, for Argon, Google's Frontier Safety report stated it could not rule out that the unmitigated model reached the cybersecurity Critical Capability Level or the biological information CCL, and it built safety cases to bring residual risk below those levels. Carbon is stronger at cyber than Argon, and the Carbon model card says Google strengthened Frontier Safety safeguards for CBRN and cyber misuse. I could not read the full Carbon Safety and Security report text, so I cannot quote its exact CCL determinations.

📊 Ingredient 6: benchmarks, with the right comparison set

Google's model card table compares Carbon to Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1. It does not include Claude Fable 5.2, which Anthropic released on November 9, one day before Carbon went GA. Here is Google's table, trimmed to the rows that matter most:

Benchmark | Carbon | Argon | GPT-6 Astra | Opus 5.5 | Fable 5.1
AA Intelligence Index v5.0 | 59 | 50 | 57 | 58 | 49
Vals Index v2.2 | 70.4% | 69.2% | 65.0% | 70.2% | n/a
FrontierSWE 2 | 61.2% | 55.0% | 65.5% | 62.3% | 56.3%
Terminal-Bench 4.0 (AA) | 65.2% | 57.1% | 59.1% | 59.6% | 52.0%
OSWorld-2.1 offline | 81.5% | 74.7% | 80.9% | 87.2% | 76.8%
AutomationBench (Zapier) | 53.9% | 51.3% | 41.4% | 42.5% | 31.4%
GraphWalks 256K-1M BFS F1 | 96.2% | 84.2% | 71.8% | 66.8% | 65.0%
Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 | 64.8% | 52.9% | 63.3% | 59.0% | 43.3%
CWE-bench | 71.0% | 68.0% | 68.0% | 67.0% | 58.0%
ExploitGym | 54.8% | 42.0% | 42.4% | 34.5% | n/a
SEC-bench Pro | 88.2% | 83.4% | 85.4% | n/a | n/a

Carbon does not lead every row even in Google's table: GPT-6 Astra leads FrontierSWE 2 and Opus 5.5 leads OSWorld. The standout is long context. GraphWalks at 256K to 1M tokens jumps from 84.2% on Argon to 96.2%, with every competitor under 72%.

One data-quality flag: RiemannBench shows 80.0% for Carbon in the model card but 72.0% on the DeepMind Gemini overview page, while Argon is listed at 76.0% in both. I could not determine which Carbon figure is current, so I would not cite either until Google reconciles them.

Now add Fable 5.2, using Anthropic's own launch table, which does include Carbon:

Benchmark | Fable 5.2 | Opus 5.5 | GPT-6 Astra | Carbon
FrontierCode 2.0 | 49.1% (Xhigh) | 45.5% | 42.8% | 41.1% (Medium)
FrontierSWE v2 | 69.9% | 62.3% | 65.5% | 61.2%
AutomationBench | 51.4% | 42.5% | 41.4% | 53.9%
Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 | 74.6% | 58.7% | 68.1% | 64.8%
OSWorld 2.1 offline, partial | 89.3% | 87.2% | 79.5% | 81.5%
AA-Briefcase v1.1 rubric | 66.1% | 61.2% | 52.0% | 61.8%
Chartography, no tools | 73.4% | 64.4% | 71.0% | 72.5%

On Anthropic's table, Fable 5.2 beats Carbon on six of the seven shared rows. Carbon keeps AutomationBench. Note the effort mismatch on FrontierCode: Fable ran at Xhigh, Carbon at Medium. At High effort Fable 5.2 scored 45.3%, still ahead of Carbon's medium run.

The two vendors also report different values for the same competitor. Google lists GPT-6 Astra at 63.3% on Terminal-Bench-Science and 80.9% on OSWorld. Anthropic lists 68.1% and 79.5%. Harness, effort and run date move these numbers by several points, so vendor tables are good for direction, not for gaps of a few points.

The independent numbers:

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0, Carbon at high reasoning scored 59 at launch, first at the time, at $7.76 per task and 21.6 minutes per task. Later reporting from AA's tracking shows Carbon at 60 and Fable 5.2 at 62 (High and Xhigh) and 65 (Max), so Carbon no longer holds the top spot. Carbon led four of the nine index evaluations: AutomationBench-AA, HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science and AA-Omniscience.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.0, Carbon in the Antigravity CLI scored 59, second behind Claude Code with Opus 5.5 at max (62). Carbon was cheaper per task and faster.

On Vals Index v2.2, Carbon at high scored 70.36% at $10.51 per test and about 47 minutes 45 seconds of latency. That was second behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 at max reasoning (70.85%) and just ahead of Opus 5.5 (70.18%). Carbon was first of 87 on Legal Research Bench.

On Arena, Carbon placed first in Text (1,528 Elo, Argon 1,520), second in Agent Arena and fourth in WebDev (1,768, up 89 points per Google).

One claim circulating on X on launch day put Carbon at about 59.3% on CursorBench 4.0 at $8.50 per task against about 56% at $9.70 for Fable 5.2. Google's blog does say Carbon ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, but I could not trace those exact figures to a primary source, so treat them as unverified.

🔍 The hallucination split

This is the most important contradiction in the launch data. Google says Carbon cuts unsupported claims by about 2x over Argon and passes 92% of its agentic honesty tasks. Artificial Analysis found that on AA-Omniscience v1.1, Carbon's accuracy rose 10 points over Argon to 58%, but its hallucination rate also rose, from 4% to 11%.

Both can be true. Google measures fabrication inside agentic deliverables. AA measures how often a model answers a knowledge question wrongly instead of abstaining, so a model that attempts more questions gets more right and more wrong. AA reports roughly 50% for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra on the same test, so 11% is still among the lowest it tracks. But Carbon says "I don't know" less often than Argon, and making things up is the most common item on one public complaint tracker so far.

💵 Ingredient 7: pricing, with worked math

Rate per 1M tokens | Intro (to Nov 30) | From Dec 1
Input | $2.00 | $4.00
Cached input (implicit, 95% off) | $0.10 | $0.20
Output, including thinking | $10.00 | $20.00

For comparison, Anthropic's list prices per 1M tokens: Claude Fable 5.2 at $8 input and $40 output, Opus 5.5 at $4 and $20, Sonnet 5.5 at $2 and $10. Carbon's intro price equals Sonnet 5.5. Its December price equals Opus 5.5. Fable 5.2 costs 2x Carbon's December rate per token and 4x its intro rate.

Worked example 1: one agentic debugging task. Assume 2,000,000 input tokens across all turns (repository context resent each turn) and 300,000 output tokens, including thinking.

No cache hits, intro: 2.0 x $2 + 0.3 x $10 = $4.00 + $3.00 = $7.00
No cache hits, December: 2.0 x $4 + 0.3 x $20 = $8.00 + $6.00 = $14.00
80% cache hits, intro: 0.4 x $2 + 1.6 x $0.10 + 0.3 x $10 = $0.80 + $0.16 + $3.00 = $3.96
80% cache hits, December: 0.4 x $4 + 1.6 x $0.20 + 0.3 x $20 = $1.60 + $0.32 + $6.00 = $7.92
Same tokens on Fable 5.2, no cache: 2.0 x $8 + 0.3 x $40 = $16 + $12 = $28.00

With caching, output is 76% of the bill, so thinking level matters more than input price.

Worked example 2: thinking level. AA measured 86.2K output tokens per task at low and 103K at medium. At December pricing that is $1.72 versus $2.06 in output, about 20% more for a 4-point index gain (54 to 58).

Worked example 3: a monthly budget. At AA's $7.76 per index task (list pricing, high), 1,000 hard tasks cost about $7,760 a month. AA measured Opus 5.5 max at $10.04 (23% more), GPT-6 Astra max at $6.25 and GPT-6.1 Sol at $1.27, on its task mix, not yours.

Worked example 4: the verbosity tax. Carbon and Argon cost the same per token, but one AA-based comparison found Carbon used roughly 1.8x Argon's tokens to run the index. A $1,000-a-month Argon workload becomes about $1,800 on Carbon. Run Argon first and move up only the tasks that fail.

🔑 Ingredient 8: who can actually use it

Surface | Who gets Carbon
Gemini API / AI Studio | Paid tier only; no free API tier mentioned
Android Studio | Via paid Gemini API
Gemini for business | API or model dropdown; also CodeMender, AlphaEvolve
Gemini app | Google AI Ultra only
AI Mode in Search | Google AI Ultra only
Google Antigravity | Google AI Ultra; /swarm in preview
AI Studio chat for subscribers | Ultra; banner reads "Unlock Gemini 4 Carbon"
Scientists | Apply for 6 months free at the top Antigravity tier, subject to selection
Cyber defenders | Fairwind Program, rolling access, specialized cyber variant

Google AI Ultra in the US comes in two tiers: Ultra 5x at $99.99 a month and Ultra 20x at $199.99 a month. AI Pro at $19.99 keeps Argon but not Carbon. Google has not said when, or whether, Carbon will reach Pro or free users. With this launch the Gemini app also removed Gemini 3.1 Pro from the picker.

Access was the loudest complaint even before GA, when Carbon topped leaderboards that almost nobody could test. On launch day the complaint became why Carbon is Ultra-only while Argon is on Pro. Paid users had already reported hitting Argon's caps after a handful of prompts, so expect pressure on Ultra 5x quotas with a model that spends more tokens per turn.

Before the blog post went up, Carbon billing SKUs appeared in Google Cloud's public catalog at $4, $20 and $0.20, the December rates, and the model was callable on Vertex AI. Confirm your invoice line before assuming the intro rate applies on Vertex.

🗣️ What early users report

Early hands-on reports, from preview testers in late October and the first users after GA, mostly agree with each other.

Slow. Preview testers on Arena called it two to four times slower than Argon depending on the task. Independent measurement puts time to first token at 12 to 23 seconds depending on thinking level. Vals measured average latency of over 47 minutes per index test. Google's own docs suggest 15-minute client timeouts.

Less lazy, more thorough. The same testers described it as noticeably better than Argon at 3D work and willing to finish jobs instead of stopping early. That matches Google's framing of extended verification loops and its claim of 29% less under-service.

Front end and UI taste are mixed. Some preview testers called the UI output weak or harsh, despite the 89-point WebDev Arena gain. One video review of 3D generations rated Carbon clearly above Argon but behind Opus 5.5 on detail and polish.

Coding agents still favor Claude. In public threads, Opus 5.5 was the most common comparison and still the working default for many coding setups.

Cheating fell, and people noticed. The Terminal-Bench 4.0 result (0.0% successful cheating, 0.4% attempts) drew the most positive developer reaction, with the caveat that a nonzero attempt rate means it still sometimes tries.

🎯 Where Carbon fits

Long-context reasoning. The GraphWalks jump to 96.2% at 256K to 1M tokens is the clearest structural advantage in any published table. Whole-repository analysis, large contract sets, multi-hundred-page technical PDFs and long log investigations are the obvious fits.

Defensive security work. Google cites 100% scanning recall and 95% triage precision on its internal Project Fortify benchmark, and Wiz reported 0-days found in two major SaaS providers in under two hours. The headline cyber benchmarks reflect Fairwind access.

Business automation and structured outputs. Carbon leads AutomationBench in both Google's and Anthropic's tables (53.9%) and leads legal research and tax agent benchmarks on Vals. Strict schema adherence for spreadsheets, decks and reports is an explicit design goal.

Science with messy data. Google's examples include diagnosing wet lab artifacts from raw data and a 40-fold average increase in remote homologs retrieved for 7 low-homolog CASP17 protein families, with broader benchmarking still underway.

Orchestrator in multi-agent setups. Google's own recommended pattern is Carbon for planning, coordination and auditing, with lighter models doing the parallel work. Given the per-task token cost, that is the economically sensible way to deploy it.

⚠️ Where it falls short

Not the top coding agent. Opus 5.5 leads AA's Coding Agent Index and Fable 5.2 leads FrontierCode and FrontierSWE. Google itself says Argon remains the right model for most software engineering.

Latency. Minutes per hard request and double-digit seconds to first token are a poor fit for chat UIs and tight edit-run loops.

Token appetite. Same per-token price as Argon, but meaningfully more tokens per task. AA flagged it as very verbose relative to the median model it tracks.

Older knowledge. A March 2026 cutoff, three months behind Anthropic's current models. Use Search grounding or URL context for anything recent.

Hallucination tradeoff. Higher accuracy came with a higher rate of confident wrong answers on AA-Omniscience compared with Argon.

Migration friction. No explicit caching, ignored sampling parameters and a combined thinking and output cap break naive Gemini 3 swaps. From Argon it is just a model ID change.

Access. Consumer use needs Ultra at $99.99 or more a month, there is no stated free API tier, and the full cyber configuration needs Fairwind vetting.

✅ Verdict

Use Carbon if your tasks are long, hard and verifiable: root-causing across large codebases, security review of code you own, reasoning across hundreds of thousands of tokens, scientific data analysis, or structured business deliverables where a wrong cell matters. Run it at medium, raise max_output_tokens to at least 32,768, set 15-minute timeouts and measure your cache hit rate in the first week. Do the heavy evaluation runs before November 30 while the price is half of list.

Stay on Argon, or route by task, if most of your traffic is interactive coding, short Q&A or latency-sensitive product features. Per token they cost the same, and per task Argon is cheaper.

Pick Claude Fable 5.2 or Opus 5.5 if coding agent quality is the only metric you care about and the budget allows it. Fable 5.2 leads most shared rows, at 2x Carbon's December per-token price. Opus 5.5 leads AA's coding agent index at the same December list price as Carbon.

Pick GPT-6 Astra or GPT-6.1 Sol if cost per completed task matters most. On AA's task mix both were cheaper.

In short, Carbon is Argon's base with more post-training for depth, a 1M-token window that holds up near its limit, a heavily documented cyber safety stack, and an intro price that undercuts Claude's top models for three weeks. It is slower and wordier than Argon and not the coding agent leader. Route your hardest tasks to it and benchmark the rest.
